analysis: The first of eleven Andrew Wyeth lots in Day 3 (3469-3479), estimated $1,000-3,000 and none of them naming a process. Day 1 carried twenty-six more. This is the same structural trap the brief identifies, one day later and at triple the estimates.
problems: Lot 1164 in Day 1 has now been proved a 1993 Aaron Ashley commercial reproduction despite a catalogue description that implied a hand process. Nothing here names a medium, an edition or a date. Out of band anyway at $1,000-2,000, but the wider point is that eleven consecutive unspecified Wyeths should be read as a consignment of reproductions until each is individually proved otherwise.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, and Wyeth reproductions are endless.

analysis: Second of the eleven-lot Day 3 Wyeth run, $1,000-2,000, process unstated.
problems: Out of band. Same reasoning as 3469 -- establish process, edition and signature or assume reproduction.

analysis: Third of the run at $2,000-3,000. The rising estimates through this block do not reflect any stated difference in medium.
problems: Out of band at twice the ceiling. Process unstated.

analysis: Fourth Wyeth, $2,000-3,000, process unstated.
problems: Out of band. Same as the rest of the block.

analysis: Fifth Wyeth, $2,000-3,000, process unstated.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Sixth Wyeth, $1,500-2,500, process unstated.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Seventh Wyeth, $1,500-2,500, process unstated.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Eighth Wyeth, $1,500-2,500, process unstated.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Ninth of the run and the dearest at $3,000-4,000. Note the catalogue gives his dates as 1917-2019, which is wrong -- Andrew Wyeth died in 2009. Small errors like that indicate the block was not catalogued by a specialist.
problems: Out of band at three to four times the ceiling, process unstated, and the artist's death date is wrong in the entry. Three of these (3477, 3478, 3479) repeat the 2019 error.

analysis: Tenth Wyeth at $2,000-3,000, same incorrect death date.
problems: Out of band, process unstated.

analysis: Last of the eleven Day 3 Wyeths and the cheapest at $1,000-1,500, with only two photographs.
problems: Out of band, just. Being the final lot of a long single-artist run is the position where a bargain would appear -- but with the process unstated and the Day 1 evidence in hand, a cheap Wyeth here is more likely a reproduction than a find.

analysis: William Thon (ME/NY/ITALY, 1906-2000) at $2,000-3,000 -- the first of four Thon lots. Thon is one of the names the brief specifically flags to watch: a Rockland artist, National Academician, and the strongest reputation in this part of Day 3. The brief also warns that his oils are out of reach and the watercolours are the affordable route.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-3,000, which confirms the brief's prediction exactly. Establish which of the four is a watercolour rather than an oil -- if any drops near the ceiling it would be the one Thon worth pursuing.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band. Thon appears regularly at Maine sales, so cheaper watercolours will come.

analysis: Second Thon at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band. Same as 3452.

analysis: Third Thon at $2,500-3,000 with six photographs.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: The major Thon at $15,000-20,000 -- fifteen to twenty times the ceiling and clearly the important canvas of the four.
problems: Far out of band. Its usefulness is positional: a five-figure Thon crossing the block concentrates the Thon money there, which marginally helps anyone bidding the three cheaper ones.

analysis: Alan Magee at $10,000-12,000, the first of four major Magee lots (3399-3402). Magee is among the most seriously collected living Maine artists -- his stone paintings are in museum collections -- and these will be originals rather than the prints at 3397 and 3398.
problems: Ten to twelve times the ceiling. The useful observation is the structure: Magee's prints at 3397 ($200-300) and 3398 ($300-400) sit immediately before four originals at $10,000-12,000, which is precisely the brief's point about works on paper being the affordable way into a collected Maine name.

analysis: Second major Magee at $10,000-12,000.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: Third major Magee at $10,000-12,000. Worth noting the current bid on this one is $500 against a $10,000 low estimate, while its three siblings are all bid at $5,000 -- almost certainly a data or entry anomaly rather than a real opportunity.
problems: Far out of band. Do not read the $500 bid as meaningful; verify against the live lot page before drawing any conclusion.

analysis: Fourth major Magee at $10,000-12,000.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: Robert Indiana at $2,000-3,000, one of four Indiana lots. Indiana lived and worked on Vinalhaven for forty years, so despite the pop-art association he is genuinely a Maine artist, and his market is national rather than regional.
problems: Out of band. Indiana's prints and multiples are also the most forged material in American pop art -- the estate litigation has muddied provenance badly. At any price, documentation matters more here than for anything else in this sale.

analysis: Second Robert Indiana at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band, same provenance caution as 3317.

analysis: Third Indiana at $3,000-5,000.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Fourth Indiana at $4,000-5,000, the dearest of the group.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: A Dennis Griggs photographic portfolio of Robert Indiana's Maine studio at $2,500-5,000. Griggs is a Topsham, Maine photographer and a documentary record of the Vinalhaven studio is genuinely interesting Maine material.
problems: Out of band. Note 3485 is a companion Griggs portfolio of William Zorach's Maine studio at the same estimate -- a matched pair of studio documentations, which is a coherent idea but priced beyond the brief.

analysis: The companion Dennis Griggs portfolio of William Zorach's Maine studio at Robinhood, Georgetown -- minutes from Bath.
problems: Out of band at $2,500-5,000.

analysis: Waldo Peirce (1884-1970) at $1,000-1,500 -- a Bangor-born Maine painter, Hemingway's friend, and a genuinely interesting figure in American modernism. The cheaper of two Peirce lots at this estimate.
problems: Out of band, though only just at the low end. Note the catalogue then lists 3427 and 3428 as 'WALDO PEIRCE (MA/UK/ITALY, 1856-1925)' -- different dates entirely, so either a second artist of the same name or a cataloguing error. Resolve which before treating any of the four as comparable.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, but worth clarifying the name confusion at preview.

analysis: Second Waldo Peirce (1884-1970) at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Out of band. Same name-confusion question as 3425.

analysis: Catalogued as 'WALDO PEIRCE (MA/UK/ITALY, 1856-1925)' at $4,000-6,000 -- dates and states that do not match the Maine Waldo Peirce of 3425 and 3426.
problems: Out of band, and the identity is unresolved in the catalogue itself. Two artists with the same name in one sale, or one artist with two sets of dates: either way the attributions on all four Peirce lots need checking before any of them means anything.

analysis: The dearest of the four Peirce lots at $8,000-12,000, with the same 1856-1925 dates as 3427.
problems: Far out of band and the same identity problem.

analysis: Marguerite Zorach (1887-1968) at $5,000-7,000. Marguerite was arguably the more radical of the two Zorachs -- an early American modernist who exhibited at the Armory Show -- and her market has risen substantially as that reassessment has taken hold. Georgetown, Maine.
problems: Out of band at five to seven times the ceiling. The Zorach consignment (3481-3485) is the strongest coherent group of Maine modernism in the sale and all of it except 3484 is beyond the budget.

analysis: William Zorach at $1,500-2,500, the middle of the three Zorach lots.
problems: Out of band. Establish medium -- at this money it is a drawing or print rather than a carving.

analysis: William Zorach at $1,500-2,000.
problems: Out of band, though 3484 at $800-1,000 is the accessible one of the three.

analysis: Andrew Winter (1893-1958), House on Monhegan Island, at $6,000-8,000. Winter was a Monhegan resident and one of the defining painters of the island -- a named Monhegan subject by a Monhegan artist is about as on-brief as Maine coastal art gets.
problems: Far out of band at six to eight times the ceiling. This is the lot I would most want if the budget were three times larger; recorded so the miss is deliberate.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band. Winter appears at Maine sales but not cheaply.

analysis: James Edward Fitzgerald (1899-1971) at $8,000-12,000. Fitzgerald took over Rockwell Kent's Monhegan house and is a major figure in the island's painting history, with a strong and rising market.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: Alexander Bower (1875-1952) at $4,000-6,000. Bower was director of the Portland Museum of Art and a competent painter of the Maine coast; his working life straddles the antique line so early work could clear 1926.
problems: Out of band at four to six times the ceiling.

analysis: Jay Connaway (1893-1970) at $2,000-3,000. Connaway lived on Monhegan for two decades and his heavy-surfaced surf paintings are among the recognisable images of the island.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Carl Sprinchorn (1887-1971) at $1,500-2,000. Sprinchorn painted the Maine woods around Monson and Katahdin rather than the coast, which makes him a slightly different proposition from the island painters -- and a genuinely distinctive one.
problems: Out of band, though closer than most. Note the catalogue misspells Sweden as 'SWEDEEN'.

analysis: Caroline Stehlin (1877-1928) at $2,000-2,500, the first of two. Her death in 1928 means essentially all her output predates the antique line -- one of the few Maine artists in Day 3 where the antique and Maine criteria genuinely coincide.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-2,500. Frustrating for the same reason as several others: right on criteria, wrong on price.

analysis: The second Caroline Stehlin at $2,000-2,500. Same reasoning as 3446.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: George Ennis (1884-1936), 'Idle Hours', at $1,000-2,000. Ennis died in 1936 so part of his output clears the antique line, and 3374 is a companion Eastport, Maine subject dated 1928.
problems: Out of band, though the low end is close. 3374 is the better of the two on criteria because it names a Maine town and a date.

analysis: George Ennis, 'Loafers', Eastport, Maine, dated 1928 -- a named Maine town and a specific year, which is unusually well documented for this section. Two years past the antique line, so modern by a whisker.
problems: Out of band at $1,000-2,000. The best-documented Ennis of the two and the one worth watching if bidding stalls near the ceiling.

analysis: The major Leo Brooks at $1,500-2,500, against 3359 at $300-400.
problems: Out of band. 3359 is the affordable Brooks and I have rated it BUY.

analysis: The major Nat Lewis at $1,500-2,500, against 3395 at $300-400.
problems: Out of band. 3395 is the affordable one.

analysis: The major Emily Muir at $2,500-3,000, against 3415 at $300-500. Muir's reputation is rising and this is presumably the substantial work of the two.
problems: Out of band. 3415 is the entry point and I have flagged it as a star.

analysis: Mary Bourke, contemporary Maine, at $1,000-1,500 -- the cheapest of three Bourke lots. Bourke has a solid current Maine gallery market.
problems: Out of band, just. Living artist with three lots in the sale, so no scarcity and gallery pricing sets the ceiling.

problems: Out of band, and a living artist selling actively through galleries -- so you would be paying retail with a premium on top.

analysis: Second Ken DeWaard at $3,000-3,500.

analysis: Eric Hopkins (ME/CT, 1951- ) at $2,000-3,000. Hopkins is a North Haven artist whose aerial island views are among the most recognisable contemporary Maine images.
problems: Out of band. Living artist with strong gallery representation, so no discount available.

analysis: Chris Huntington (ME/OH, 1938- ) at $2,000-3,000. A Bowdoinham painter with a long Maine career.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Erik Minzner, contemporary Maine, at $1,000-2,000.

analysis: Alison Rector, contemporary Maine, at $1,500-2,500. Her quiet architectural interiors have a distinct following.

analysis: John Paul Caponigro (ME/MA, 1965- ) at $1,000-1,200. A digital-media artist and the son of photographer Paul Caponigro, based in Cushing, Maine.
problems: Out of band. Digital prints also have the weakest resale of any contemporary medium because editions can be reprinted.

analysis: Henrik Martin Meyer (NH/CT/ME, 1908-1972) at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Out of band. Triple-state attribution, so the Maine association is one of three.

analysis: Abraham Jacob Bogdanov (1887-1946) at $1,500-2,000 with eight photographs -- unusually good disclosure. A New Hampshire and Russian painter whose early work could clear the antique line.
problems: Out of band. No Maine connection.

analysis: An impressionist portrait of a woman signed 'McManus' at $1,000-1,500. Per the standing principles this is an unidentified signature -- the cataloguer saw a name and could not place it -- so it should not attract named-maker money.
problems: Out of band, and the attribution is a surname with no dates, no state and no first name. Price it as an anonymous decorative portrait, which is well below the estimate.

analysis: A circa-1925 portrait of a gypsy girl, unsigned, at $1,500-2,500. Catalogued to a year that sits right on the antique line, and anonymous so no maker premium.
problems: Out of band. Only two photographs for a four-figure painting. The subject type -- romanticised 'gypsy girl' -- was mass-produced as decorative art through the 1920s and 30s, which is why it is unsigned.

analysis: An unidentified mid-century Abstract Expressionist painting from the John Nicholas Brown collection at $10,000-20,000. The provenance is the entire value proposition -- a distinguished Rhode Island collection -- since the artist is unknown.
problems: Far out of band. An unattributed AbEx canvas carrying a five-figure estimate on provenance alone is a speculative proposition: the buyer is betting the attribution can be established. Not a criteria fit in any case.
